Bayesian statistics

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics Statistical inference
OurBigBook.com Words: 11k Articles: 180
Bayesian statistics expresses uncertainty about an unknown statistical parameter through a probability distribution, then uses Bayes' theorem to update it after observing data. The prior distribution describes uncertainty before the current observations; the likelihood function describes how the statistical model generates those observations at each parameter value; the posterior distribution describes uncertainty conditional on the observations and that model. A physical parameter can have one fixed value while its value remains uncertain to us. Assigning it a probability distribution represents that uncertainty under the chosen model, rather than requiring the physical parameter to change randomly between measurements.
For example, suppose ten Bernoulli trials are independent conditional on an unknown heads probability θ, with a beta distribution prior Beta(2,2). Eight heads and two tails give the posterior distribution Beta(10,4) by Beta-binomial conjugacy. Its posterior mean is 10/14=5/7≈0.714286, between the prior mean 1/2 and observed binomial proportion 8/10. The Bayesian posterior below computes the whole update, and the credible interval below summarizes its remaining uncertainty. The conjugate update is explained in MIT 18.05, Reading 15: beta and normal conjugate priors.
The useful feature is that one posterior distribution supports several questions: a posterior mean estimates a value, a credible interval reports a range, and a posterior predictive distribution predicts a future observation while averaging over parameter uncertainty. With conditionally independent new data, today's posterior distribution can become tomorrow's prior distribution. These conclusions remain conditional on the statistical model and prior distribution; a precise update does not establish that either assumption fits the experiment.
A historical starting point is Thomas Bayes's essay in the 1763 volume of the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions, communicated after his death by Richard Price. Its opening problem asks for uncertainty about an unknown event probability given observed successes and failures: the same direction of reasoning illustrated by the coin example. See Bayes and Price, An Essay towards solving a Problem in the Doctrine of Chances, opening letter and problem.

Credible set (P(θ∈C∣x)=1−α)

Words: 70
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
A credible set is a measurable set of parameter values containing specified posterior probability. At credibility level 1−α, it satisfies ∫C​π(θ∣x)dθ=1−α for a continuous posterior. A credible interval is a credible set that is an interval. Equal-tailed and highest-density choices add selection rules; the posterior-mass requirement alone does not make the set unique. Its probability statement is conditional on the observed data and prior model, whereas a frequentist confidence interval is interpreted through repeated-sample coverage.

Selection conditioning in Bayesian inference (p(θ∣d,S)=p(θ∣d) when S depends only on conditioned data)

Words: 81
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
If inclusion depends only on fully observed data d, then p(S∣d,θ)=p(S∣d) cancels from Bayes' theorem for that individual's parameters. Selection can still matter for unknown population parameters and for missing or unconditioned features. For independent detected observations conditional on their count and population parameters Λ, each likelihood has normalization α(Λ)=∫S(d)p(d∣Λ)dd. A model for the detected count adds its own count likelihood. Do not combine a selected-population prior with a truncated-data likelihood in a way that counts the same selection twice.

Likelihood reconstruction from posterior simulation

Words: 74
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
For data x, a positive prior distribution density π and likelihood function ℓ, Bayes' theorem gives posterior density h(θ∣x)=π(θ)ℓ(θ)/m(x). Thus h/π reconstructs the likelihood up to a constant. Estimate the posterior density from simulation, divide by the known prior density and maximize over the search region. A posterior mode alone instead estimates a maximum a posteriori estimate; it estimates a likelihood maximizer only when the prior is constant there. Prior support must include the likelihood maximizer of interest.

BUGS

Words: 83 Articles: 1
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
BUGS specifies a probabilistic model through stochastic nodes, deterministic nodes and observed data, then uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to simulate its Bayesian posterior. Its normal sampling notation uses a precision parameter rather than a variance, and its gamma notation uses shape and rate.

Zeros trick

Words: 47
BUGS OurBigBook.com
A zeros trick implements a positive likelihood function L(θ) by adding an observed zero with Poisson distribution mean K−logL(θ). If this mean is nonnegative throughout the parameter support, its likelihood is e−KL(θ) and yields the intended Bayesian posterior. The constant K must be independent of the parameter; arbitrary clipping changes the target.

Variational inference

Words: 272 Articles: 5
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution by minimizing a Kullback-Leibler divergence over a chosen family of probability distributions. For an unnormalized posterior density h and a trial probability density function q, minimizing Eq​[logq−logh] is equivalent to minimizing KL(q∥h/∫h).

Combined score and pathwise gradient estimator (∇λ​Esλ​​Wλ​=Esλ​​[Wλ​∇λ​logsλ​+∇λ​Wλ​])

Words: 85
Variational inference OurBigBook.com
Under fixed-support regularity permitting differentiation under the integral sign, apply the product rule to ∫sλ​Wλ​. The first derivative term is ∫Wλ​∇sλ​=E[Wλ​∇logsλ​] and the second is E[∇Wλ​]. This proves the displayed identity. For an evidence lower bound, take Wλ​=logp(tλ​(ε),x)−logqλ​(tλ​(ε)), holding noise ε fixed in the inner derivatives. Parameter-independent continuous noise contributes a reparameterization gradient; untransformed discrete choices contribute a score-function gradient estimator. A mixed base law cannot be called parameter independent if its discrete factors retain variational parameters.[ref]

Guide program

Words: 42
Variational inference OurBigBook.com
A guide program is a probabilistic program whose generated probability distribution approximates a model's posterior distribution. Its adjustable parameters are fitted by variational inference. The guide must assign probability only where the target allows it when minimizing DKL​(q∥p), but a tractable guide can still miss important target regions.

Reparameterization gradient

Words: 37
Variational inference OurBigBook.com
A reparameterization gradient differentiates an expected value by representing the simulated random variable as a differentiable transformation of parameter-independent noise. For Xη​=gη​(ε), the identity ∇η​E[Fη​(Xη​)]=E[∇η​Fη​(gη​(ε))] requires justified differentiation under the integral sign. For a normal distribution, use X=m+eρε with ε drawn from the standard normal distribution.

Markov chain variational inference

Words: 33
Variational inference OurBigBook.com
Markov chain variational inference optimizes an initial parametric probability distribution νη​ by minimizing KL(Ktνη​∥π) after a fixed number of Markov kernel updates. The best initial probability distribution can depend on t; Kullback-Leibler divergence contraction does not imply that optimization commutes with applying the Markov kernel.

Mean-field variational inference (q(x)=∏i​qi​(xi​))

Words: 42
Variational inference OurBigBook.com
Mean-field variational inference restricts the trial probability density function to q(x)=∏i​qi​(xi​). With the other factors fixed, qj∗​(xj​)∝exp(Eq−j​​logπ(xj​,X−j​)), provided this expression has a finite positive normalization constant. Subtracting the objective at qj∗​ leaves KL(qj​∥qj∗​)≥0, proving the update is optimal when the terms are well defined.

Data augmentation

Words: 18
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
Data augmentation enlarges a posterior distribution with latent variables whose removal by marginalization recovers the original posterior distribution. Convenient full conditional distributions then permit a Gibbs sampler on the enlarged space.

Hierarchical Bayesian model

Words: 490 Articles: 7
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
A hierarchical Bayesian model assigns distributions to local latent variables conditional on shared hyperparameters, then distributions to observations conditional on those latent variables. Its probabilistic graphical model records this conditional factorization, often using a plate for repeated observations. Integrating out latent variables gives the marginal likelihood of the hyperparameters. Priors described as flat on logarithms require a Jacobian determinant when densities are written in the original positive variables.

Conditional exchangeability of hospital risks

Words: 76
Hierarchical Bayesian model OurBigBook.com
Unknown hospital event probabilities can be modelled as exchangeable random variables conditional on shared hyperparameters, for example Pj​∣m,κ∼Beta(mκ,(1−m)κ) independently. Different sample sizes affect the binomial observations but do not by themselves invalidate exchangeability of the risks. Known systematic covariate differences, such as case mix or procedure type, should instead enter the risk model; only residual effects may then be exchangeable. Exchangeability permits heterogeneous realized risks and is not an assertion that all risks are equal.

Non-centered Gaussian random-effect parameterization (αi​=δ+τzi​,zi​∼N(0,1))

Words: 77
Hierarchical Bayesian model OurBigBook.com
A normal local effect αi​∣δ,τ∼N(δ,τ2) can be represented by a standardized latent variable zi​∼N(0,1) independent of the hyperparameters, with αi​=δ+τzi​. This preserves the hierarchical model while changing the coordinates explored by Markov chain Monte Carlo. It often improves mixing when individual effects are weakly informed, reducing strong scale-effect dependence. Centered coordinates can be better with very informative individual data. The stochastic prior on zi​ implements the transformation correctly; re-expressing an existing density directly instead requires the appropriate Jacobian determinant.

Partial pooling

Words: 49
Hierarchical Bayesian model OurBigBook.com
Partial pooling estimates related local parameters jointly through shared hyperparameters. Each local Bayesian posterior balances its own likelihood function against a group prior distribution, with stronger shrinkage when its data are weak or the group variation is small. It lies between forcing all local parameters to be equal and estimating them independently. Random-effects meta-analysis is an important application.

Gamma–Poisson hierarchical model

Words: 118 Articles: 2
Hierarchical Bayesian model OurBigBook.com
A Gamma–Poisson hierarchical model uses Yi​∣θi​∼Poisson(ti​θi​), θi​∣b∼Gamma(a,b), and b∼Gamma(c,r), with gamma distributions in shape-rate convention. Conditional independence gives full conditional distributions θi​∣b,y∼Gamma(a+yi​,b+ti​) and b∣θ,y∼Gamma(c+na,r+∑i​θi​).

Poisson–exponential posterior shrinkage formula (E[θi​∣y]=s+ns​yi​+s+nn​y​)

Words: 55
Gamma–Poisson hierarchical model OurBigBook.com
For Yi​∣θi​∼Poisson(θi​) and θi​∣ψ∼Exp(ψ), a scale-invariant prior dψ/ψ induces the Haldane prior on ϕ=(1+ψ)−1. Integrating out each local mean gives p(yi​∣ϕ)=(1−ϕ)ϕyi​. Thus ϕ∣y∼Beta(s,n) for s=∑i​yi​>0. The gamma full conditional distribution has mean (yi​+1)ϕ, so the tower property gives (yi​+1)s/(s+n), equal to the displayed partial pooling formula. For s=0, the posterior is improper and this expectation is undefined.

Gamma-integrated baseline Poisson likelihood (p(y∣β)∝e∑k​yk​ηk​/(b+∑k​eηk​)n+a)

Words: 43
Gamma–Poisson hierarchical model OurBigBook.com
For independent Poisson distributions with means ueηk​ and a shape–rate Gamma distribution prior on u, integrating u adds a to the total-count exponent and b to the sum of relative rates. This distinguishes gamma mixing from conditioning on the total count, which gives a multinomial distribution.

Gaussian–exponential hierarchical colour model

Words: 109
Hierarchical Bayesian model OurBigBook.com
An observed astronomical colour is the sum of a normal intrinsic colour, a nonnegative dust contribution with an exponential distribution, and normal measurement noise. With latent Cs​∼N(μ,v), Es​∼Exp(mean τ) and Os​∣Cs​,Es​∼N(Cs​+Es​,rs​), the Gibbs sampler conditionals for Cs​ are normal and those for Es​ are truncated normal distributions. A flat prior on μ and inverse-gamma priors on v,τ give inverse-gamma conditional updates for the two scales. Log-flat priors on both scales instead make the joint posterior improper when all rs​>0, despite formally proper full conditionals at generic latent states: the marginal observed likelihood has a positive limit at either zero-scale boundary. Proper positive-scale priors restore a genuine joint posterior.

Maximum a posteriori estimation

Words: 70 Articles: 1
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
Maximum a posteriori estimation selects a parameter value maximizing its posterior density relative to a specified reference measure. Its output is a maximum a posteriori estimate. The maximizing value need not be invariant under a nonlinear reparameterization, because a density transforms with a Jacobian.

Maximum a posteriori estimate

Words: 33
Maximum a posteriori estimation OurBigBook.com
A maximum a posteriori estimate maximizes the posterior density of a parameter or latent configuration. Equivalently, it maximizes the sum of the log likelihood and log prior, relative to the chosen reference measure.

Credible interval (P(Θ∈C(d)∣D=d)=1−α)

Words: 610 Articles: 4
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
A credible interval is an interval C(d) containing a prescribed amount 1−α of posterior probability for an unknown scalar statistical parameter Θ. For a continuous posterior distribution with posterior density p(θ∣d), its endpoints satisfy
P(a≤Θ≤b∣D=d)=∫ab​p(θ∣d)dθ=1−α.
(1)
The conditioning includes the chosen statistical model and prior distribution. For a discrete posterior distribution, exact equality may be impossible because of its probability masses; an interval can instead be required to contain at least the requested posterior probability. An interval compresses the full posterior distribution into a range whose uncertainty can be communicated in the parameter's own units. See MIT 18.05, Class 16: probability intervals.
For the eight-head, two-tail example in Bayesian statistics, the posterior density is 2860θ9(1−θ)3 on [0,1]. Its cumulative distribution function, obtained by integration of this polynomial, is
F(t)=286t10−780t11+715t12−220t13,0≤t≤1.
(2)
Solving F(a)=0.025 and F(b)=0.975 by the bisection method gives
a≈0.461868461,b≈0.909079605,F(b)−F(a)=0.95.
(3)
These are numerical approximations to the exact quantiles defined by those equations; the endpoints were computed from the cumulative distribution function, rather than read off a plot. The resulting equal-tailed credible interval leaves 2.5% posterior probability on each side. Its shaded area is 95% of the total area under the posterior density.
Credible intervals are not unique. The one-sided credible interval [0,F−1(0.95)]≈[0,0.887334219] also has 95% posterior probability, but leaves all 5% outside it on the right. A highest density region instead selects points above a density threshold; it need not be an equal-tailed credible interval, and when the posterior density has separated peaks it need not be one interval at all. Thus a reported credible interval should specify its construction.
A 95% credible interval makes a statement about the statistical parameter conditional on these observed data and the Bayesian model. A 95% confidence interval instead refers to the coverage probability of a procedure under repeated sampling at a fixed parameter value. These are different conditioning statements: 95% posterior probability does not by itself imply 95% coverage probability for every fixed parameter. The confidence interval article develops that sampling interpretation.

Highest posterior density interval ([a,b]={θ:π(θ∣x)≥k})

Words: 217 Articles: 1
Credible interval OurBigBook.com
A highest posterior density interval is a credible interval whose included points have at least as high posterior density as excluded points, apart from boundary and null-set choices. It is a highest density region of prescribed posterior probability that happens to be an interval. For a continuous unimodal posterior with two interior endpoints, the endpoint densities agree. A monotone posterior on a half-line instead starts at a support boundary, as in a Pareto highest density interval. For a multimodal posterior distribution, the highest-density region can be disconnected and cannot always be represented by a single interval. Density-level regions use a specified parameter coordinate and reference measure; they are not generally preserved by nonlinear reparametrization.

Beta highest posterior density endpoint characterization (FA,B​(u)−FA,B​(l)=1−α,fA,B​(l)=fA,B​(u))

Words: 120
Highest posterior density interval OurBigBook.com
For a beta distribution with shape parameters A,B>1, the probability density function vanishes at zero and one and is strictly increasing up to m=(A−1)/(A+B−2) and strictly decreasing afterwards. This follows because the derivative of its logarithm is (A−1)/t−(B−1)/(1−t), whose sign changes at m.
For each 0<α<1, the highest posterior density interval when this beta distribution is a posterior distribution has unique endpoints 0<l<m<u<1 determined by
FA,B​(u)−FA,B​(l)=1−α,lA−1(1−l)B−1=uA−1(1−u)B−1.
(4)
The second equation gives equal endpoint posterior densities. For every density threshold strictly between zero and the modal height there is precisely one crossing on each side. The enclosed probability is continuous and strictly decreasing from one to zero as the threshold increases, proving existence, uniqueness and the highest posterior density interval property. The restrictions A,B>1 are essential to this two-interior-endpoint characterization; monotone cases use a support boundary instead.

Equal-tailed credible interval ([F−1(α/2),F−1(1−α/2)])

Words: 51
Credible interval OurBigBook.com
An equal-tailed credible interval uses quantiles of a continuous posterior distribution to leave posterior probability α/2 in each tail. It is also called a central credible interval; central refers to equal tail probabilities, not equal distances from the posterior mean. For the beta distribution Beta(10,4) in credible interval, the 95% endpoints are approximately 0.461868461 and 0.909079605, whose midpoint 0.685474033 differs from the posterior mean 5/7.

One-sided credible interval ((−∞,F−1(1−α)])

Words: 56
Credible interval OurBigBook.com
A one-sided credible interval puts all excluded posterior probability in one tail. For a continuous posterior distribution, an upper bound u=F−1(1−α) satisfies P(Θ≤u∣D=d)=1−α; a lower bound uses F−1(α). Intersecting with the parameter's allowed range removes points of zero posterior probability. For the beta distribution Beta(10,4), the upper 95% bound is u≈0.887334219, so [0,u] is the alternative credible interval shown above.

A Dirichlet process is a distribution over probability measures such that the masses assigned to every finite measurable partition have a Dirichlet distribution. Its draws are almost surely discrete.

A Dirichlet prior with parameters (α1​,…,αK​) combined with categorical labels having counts (N1​,…,NK​) gives a Dirichlet posterior with parameters (α1​+N1​,…,αK​+NK​).

Prior probability (Π(A)=P(Θ∈A))

Words: 498 Articles: 7
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
Prior probability describes uncertainty before the current observations are incorporated. For a statistical parameter Θ, a prior distribution assigns probabilities to its possible ranges, conditional on background information and a statistical model. A continuous prior density π(θ) specifies these probabilities through integration:
P(Θ∈A)=∫A​π(θ)dθ,π(θ)≥0,∫π(θ)dθ=1.
(5)
Here the probability density function is relative to Lebesgue measure dθ; a discrete prior distribution instead uses a probability mass function and sums. Density at one point is not the probability of that point. A nonnegative kernel with infinite total mass is an improper prior, whose use requires a separate check of posterior propriety.
For the coin model in Bayesian statistics, the beta distribution Beta(2,2) has prior density π(θ)=6θ(1−θ) on [0,1]. Its mean is 1/2 and its variance is 1/20. It favors moderate heads probabilities without ruling out values near zero or one. For example,
P(Θ>3/4)=∫3/41​6θ(1−θ)dθ=325​=0.15625.

The prior curve in Bayesian posterior makes this preference visible; moment matching for a beta prior explains how to choose a beta distribution from a desired mean and variance.
A prior distribution lets earlier evidence or elicited knowledge contribute to statistical inference when the current sample size is limited. It also exposes assumptions that can be checked by prior elicitation and a prior predictive check. Before the same eight heads and two tails, a uniform prior Beta(1,1) would give posterior mean 9/12=3/4, compared with 5/7 under Beta(2,2): the observations do not uniquely determine a Bayesian posterior. Even a uniform prior makes a choice of parameter coordinates; its child article explains why changing coordinates can destroy uniformity.

The strict positive, finite condition is essential: a zero or infinite normalizer does not define this posterior distribution, even if the unnormalized expression can be written down. Other reference measures give the corresponding density formula; discrete parameter values replace the integral by a sum. The posterior propriety article gives examples where normalization fails.
With d fixed, L(θ;d)=p(d∣θ) is a likelihood function of θ. Its normalization as a sampling distribution is over possible data, not over parameter values. In particular, a likelihood function is not a probability density function for Θ and need not integrate to one over θ. The prior density supplies the probability weighting, and the Bayesian model evidence normalizes their product. This distinction prevents a tempting mistake: reversing the conditioning merely by exchanging the words “data” and “parameter”.

If the data are instead one particular ordered sequence with eight heads and two tails, its likelihood function omits the factor 45 and its Bayesian model evidence becomes 3/1430. The factor cancels in Bayes' theorem, leaving the same posterior distribution; these two data descriptions have different sampling probabilities but identical information about θ here.
The prior density and posterior density use the left axis and each integrate to one. The dashed likelihood function uses the right axis and is divided by its maximum solely to compare its shape; it is not a parameter probability density function. The likelihood function peaks at 8/10, while the posterior mode is 9/12=3/4 and the posterior mean is 5/7. Multiplying by the prior density shifts the preferred values toward one half while preserving a range of possibilities.
The resulting posterior variance is 10⋅4/(142⋅15)=2/147≈0.0136054, compared with prior variance 1/20. In this example the update reduces uncertainty. The posterior predictive probability of heads on the next conditionally independent toss is E[Θ∣D=8]=5/7, and the credible interval above reports a 95% range. These are summaries of the same posterior distribution, rather than competing estimates of one density peak.

Coupling from the past uses a fixed two-sided sequence of random update maps for a finite Markov chain. Increase a backward horizon until the composition from that horizon to time zero sends every starting state to the same state. Retain the maps at previously exposed times. The resulting common image is an exact stationary sample. If a length-m block has positive probability ε of mapping every state to one state, independent disjoint blocks imply failure to coalesce by horizon T has probability at most (1−ε)⌊T/m⌋. For a deterministic horizon, a stationary initial state yields a stationary final state, and agrees with the algorithm's output on coalescence. Letting the deterministic horizon tend to infinity proves the output has the stationary law without conditioning on a random stopping horizon.

Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
For a standard bivariate normal distribution with correlation ρ, each conditional has variance 1−ρ2 and mean ρ times the other coordinate. A sweep draws Xn+1​=ρYn​+1−ρ2​Z1​, then Yn+1​=ρXn+1​+1−ρ2​Z2​. The resulting coordinate chain is an AR(1) process with coefficient ρ2 and innovation variance 1−ρ4. It shows explicitly why near-unit correlation slows successive Gibbs sweeps.

WinBUGS

Words: 50
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
Software for Bayesian inference through Markov chain Monte Carlo in directed statistical models. Its model language uses dnorm(mean, precision), so the second argument is inverse variance; dcat indexes a supplied probability vector, and dbern introduces a binary latent variable. The model is declarative, so the order of deterministic node definitions does not impose procedural evaluation order.

Linear contraction of a two-coordinate Gaussian Gibbs sweep (bk+1​−μb​=ADC2​(bk​−μb​)+ηk​)

Words: 55
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
For Gaussian precision (AC​CD​), a systematic update of the first coordinate followed by the second makes the centered second coordinate an AR(1) chain with coefficient C2/(AD)<1. Independent conditional Gaussian noise supplies its stable innovation. This proves convergence of the Gaussian Gibbs sampler and explains slower mixing when posterior correlation has magnitude near one.

Gibbs sampling for a finite hidden spin field

Words: 76 Articles: 1
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
For a strictly positive posterior on finitely many binary spins, a Random-scan Gibbs sampler uses the two local posterior weights to redraw one spin. Positive full conditional distribution probabilities allow every finite sequence of spin changes, giving an irreducible Markov chain with positive self-transition probabilities.
Local likelihood factors in a hidden spin field
Words: 40
Gibbs sampling for a finite hidden spin field OurBigBook.com
When an observation mean depends on the neighboring spins, changing a spin affects observations centered at its neighbors. Its own observation need not involve that spin. Selecting precisely the affected factors gives a correct local full conditional distribution without recomputing the entire posterior.

Systematic Gibbs sampling need not be reversible

Words: 36
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
Every full-conditional coordinate update satisfies detailed balance with the target distribution. Their systematic ordered composition preserves the target but need not satisfy detailed balance, since compositions of reversible kernels need not be reversible. A fixed-probability random-scan mixture remains reversible.

Blocked Gibbs sampler

Words: 70 Articles: 1
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A blocked Gibbs sampler draws groups of coordinates jointly from their full conditional distributions. Each update preserves the joint probability distribution; dependence between blocks can still cause a long mixing time.
Checkerboard Gibbs sampling
Words: 47
Blocked Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
On a bipartite image graph, the pixels of one color are conditionally independent given the other color. Draw all black pixels from their independent full conditionals, then draw all whites conditional on the new blacks. Each color update preserves the target law, so their composition does too.

Random-scan Gibbs sampler

Words: 77 Articles: 1
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A random-scan Gibbs sampler chooses one coordinate, commonly uniformly at random, and redraws it from its complete conditional distribution while leaving all other coordinates fixed. Each coordinate update preserves the target distribution.
Detailed balance of a random-scan Gibbs sampler
Words: 45
Random-scan Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A single-coordinate Gibbs sampler update preserves the remaining coordinates and independently redraws the selected coordinate from its full conditional distribution. The joint measure of old and new states factors into a marginal and two identical conditional factors, making it symmetric. A fixed-probability mixture of such kernels therefore satisfies detailed balance.

Tempered Gibbs sampler

Words: 36
Gibbs sampler OurBigBook.com
A tempered Gibbs sampler changes the coordinate-selection probabilities and compensates by drawing from modified complete conditionals. Its invariant law can differ from the desired target, so expectations under the target are recovered with explicit importance weights.

For independent Zi​∣μ,ω∼N(μ,ω−1), a flat prior on μ, and an exponential prior of rate λ on ω, the full conditionals are
μ∣ω,z∼N(zˉ,nω1​),

and
ω∣μ,z∼Gamma(2n​+1,λ+21​∑i​(zi​−μ)2),

Bayesian model evidence (Z)

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Bayesian statistics OurBigBook.com
The Bayesian model evidence is the prior predictive distribution evaluated at the data D. For a statistical model Hj​ with a normalized prior density πj​, its marginal likelihood is
mj​(D)=p(D∣Hj​)=Zj​=∫p(D∣θj​,Hj​)πj​(θj​∣Hj​)dθj​.
(33)
This is an expected value of the likelihood function under the prior distribution; for discrete statistical parameters, replace the integral by a sum. For continuous observations, mj​(D) is a probability density function value with respect to a specified data reference measure, rather than a probability of one exact observation. Comparisons must use the same data and reference measure. The same mj​(D) normalizes the within-model Bayesian posterior and supplies the between-model comparison in a Bayes factor.[ref]
A normalized prior distribution makes the Bayesian model evidence an average, so it cannot exceed the largest likelihood function value on its support. A broad prior distribution can assign little mass to values that predict the data well, even when one value gives an excellent fit. The worked uniform-alternative binomial Bayes factor below makes the difference between averaging and maximum likelihood estimation explicit.

Evidence averaging under an interval prior (Z=(b−a)−1∫ab​L(θ)dθ)

Words: 99 Articles: 1
Bayesian model evidence OurBigBook.com
For a normalized uniform prior on [a,b], Bayesian model evidence is Z=(b−a)−1∫ab​L(θ)dθ. It averages the likelihood over the prior range. Extending a well-placed interval into low-likelihood regions reduces that average, but moving or widening a poorly placed interval can improve it. A model prior is separate: posterior model odds equal the evidence ratio multiplied by prior model odds.

Laplace-likelihood interval evidence (Z/C=(s/w)(1−e−w/s))

Words: 44
Evidence averaging under an interval prior OurBigBook.com
If L(θ)=Ce−∣θ−μ∣/s, integrate the two exponential branches at μ. An interval of half-width w centred at μ has Z/C=(s/w)(1−e−w/s). An interval entirely below the peak has Z/C=s[e(b−μ)/s−e(a−μ)/s]/(b−a). These expressions show quantitatively how fit location and prior width combine.

Prior predictive check

Words: 53
Bayesian model evidence OurBigBook.com
A prior predictive check simulates parameters from the prior distribution and observations from their sampling model, then examines whether those observations are plausible before conditioning on data. This reveals unintended information from apparently broad priors, especially after nonlinear transformations or when scales and correlations are coupled. It differs from a posterior predictive check, which uses the posterior distribution.

Harmonic mean estimator of Bayesian model evidence

Words: 34
Bayesian model evidence OurBigBook.com
Given posterior draws θi​, the harmonic mean estimator is
Z=[m1​∑i=1m​L(θi​)−1]−1.
(34)
Although the average inside brackets estimates Z−1, its variance is often infinite because reciprocal likelihoods grow rapidly in the posterior tails.

Bayes factor (B01​)

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Bayesian model evidence OurBigBook.com
A Bayes factor measures how data change the relative support for two specified statistical models. Write mj​(D)=p(D∣Hj​) for their Bayesian model evidence and define the direction explicitly:
BF10​(D)=m0​(D)m1​(D)​.
(35)
For positive finite m0​(D),m1​(D), a value above one favors H1​ over H0​; a value below one favors H0​ over H1​. Reversing the comparison gives B01​=BF01​=1/BF10​, the opposite direction used in some formulas below.
For mutually exclusive, exhaustive H0​,H1​ with positive prior probabilities, divide their two Bayes' theorem formulas. Their common data normalizer cancels, leaving
posterior oddsP(H0​∣D)P(H1​∣D)​​​=BF10​m0​(D)m1​(D)​​​prior oddsP(H0​)P(H1​)​​​.
(36)
The Bayes factor therefore multiplies prior odds into posterior odds. It is evidence conditional on the specified statistical models and their within-model prior distributions; it is not P(H1​∣D). Model prior probabilities supply a separate input.[ref]
For an original stipulated example, consider ten independent and identically distributed Bernoulli trials, with heads as success. Compare H0​:p=0.4 with H1​:p=0.7, both fixed before seeing the data. Take D to be one particular ordered sequence containing eight heads and two tails. The likelihood function under either point model is p8(1−p)2, so
BF10​=0.480.620.780.32​=(0.40.7​)8(0.60.3​)2=2621445764801​≈21.9909706.
(37)
If P(H1​)=0.1, the prior odds for H1​ against H0​ are 1/9. Hence the posterior odds are 21.9909706/9≈2.4434412, and
P(H1​∣D)=9+BF10​BF10​​=81240975764801​≈0.7095928.
(38)
Equal model prior probabilities would instead give BF10​/(1+BF10​)≈0.956505. The same Bayes factor can thus accompany different posterior probabilities. These statements condition on the two-model comparison; they do not establish that either statistical model describes a real coin.
Using the heads count K=8 instead of the ordered sequence changes the sample space. The binomial distribution assigns it mass (810​)p8(1−p)2. The same binomial coefficient multiplies both models' Bayesian model evidence and cancels in their Bayes factor. Mixing an ordered-sequence numerator with a count denominator would introduce an erroneous factor of 45.
Fix the candidate statistical models, their parameter prior distributions, and model prior probabilities before using the current data for this update. The Bayes factor is useful because it separates evidence from model prior odds, but it still depends on the parameter prior distributions. An improper prior has an arbitrary multiplicative normalization: multiplying its kernel by c multiplies its formal marginal likelihood by c, even if the within-model posterior distribution is normalizable. Without a separately justified convention, the ordinary Bayes factor is then undefined up to arbitrary constants.[ref]

Bayes factor for the sign of a normal mean (B01​=Φ(−z)/Φ(z))

Words: 119
Bayes factor OurBigBook.com
For a random sample Xi​∣θ∼N(θ,σ2) with known σ>0 and prior distribution θ∼N(0,τ2) with τ>0, compare H0​:θ<0 to H1​:θ≥0. The prior odds are one by symmetry. Normal-normal conjugacy gives a normal posterior distribution with
μn​=σ2+nτ2nτ2X​,vn​=σ2+nτ2σ2τ2​.
(39)
Its negative and nonnegative masses are Φ(−z) and Φ(z), where
z=vn​​μn​​=σσ2+nτ2​nτX​.
(40)
Since the Bayes factor is the posterior odds divided by the prior odds,
B01​=Φ(z)Φ(−z)​.​
(41)
Here Φ is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. The ratio decreases with the sample mean. For any threshold b>0, the inequality B01​<b is equivalent to Φ(z)>1/(1+b) and hence to
X>nτσσ2+nτ2​​Φ−1(1+b1​).
(42)
For b=1/10, the quantile is Φ−1(10/11)≈1.33518, and the equivalent posterior probability threshold for H0​ is 1/11. The symmetry and proper normalization of the two hypothesis-conditional priors are essential to replacing the Bayes factor by the posterior odds directly.

Equal likelihoods preserve model odds (P(D∣H1​)=P(D∣H2​)⇒O12​(D)=O12​)

Words: 45
Bayes factor OurBigBook.com
For two models with finite positive prior odds, a sequence of data with identical conditional likelihoods under both models has Bayes factor one. The posterior odds therefore equal the prior odds. This requires equality of the probability model for all the data considered, not merely that both models fit a selected data set.

Uniform-alternative binomial Bayes factor (B01​(y)=(n+1)(yn​)2−n)

Words: 405
Bayes factor OurBigBook.com
For a binomial distribution count, compare a point null θ=1/2 with the uniform alternative prior distribution on (0,1). The alternative Bayesian model evidence is
(yn​)∫01​θy(1−θ)n−ydθ=n+11​,
(43)
so the exact Bayes factor favouring the point null is (n+1)(yn​)2−n. With standardized deviation z=2(y−n/2)/n​, the local normal distribution approximation is B01​≈2n/π​e−z2/2. At fixed z the frequentist p-value remains approximately constant, while the factor grows like n​. This demonstrates the prior-width mechanism behind the Jeffreys-Lindley paradox for a Gaussian point null in a discrete sampling model.
For a separate original example, change the point null to H0​:p=1/2 and take HU​ to have a uniform prior p∼Beta(1,1), fixed before the ten Bernoulli trials. Here p is drawn once under HU​ and shared by all ten trials: they are independent conditional on p. For one particular ordered sequence with eight heads and two tails, the Euler beta function gives
m0​(D)=2−10,mU​(D)=∫01​p8(1−p)2dp=B(9,3)=11!8!2!​=4951​.
(44)
Thus the Bayes factor for the uniform alternative against the point null is
BFU0​=4951024​≈2.0686869,B0U​=1024495​≈0.4833984.
(45)
The binomial distribution count formulation gives m0​(K=8)=45/1024 and mU​(K=8)=45/495=1/11. Their ratio is again 1024/495; these count masses must not be combined with the ordered-sequence masses above. The general B01​ formula at the start of this article puts the point null in the numerator, so it equals B0U​ here.
In contrast, maximum likelihood estimation gives p​=0.8: differentiating the log-likelihood yields 8/p−2/(1−p)=0, and the endpoints have zero likelihood. Its peak-to-null likelihood ratio is
L(0.5)L(0.8)​=2−100.880.22​≈6.8719477.
(46)
This peak is chosen after seeing the data, so it is not the Bayes factor of the prespecified HU​. The Bayesian model evidence for HU​ averages L(p) over its entire uniform prior; it is smaller than the peak. It is also smaller than L(0.7)=0.780.32≈0.00518832. Against the same p=0.5 null, a point alternative fixed at p=0.7 would give a Bayes factor about 5.31284, greater than 2.06869. An integrated alternative need not outperform a point alternative.
For a general proper beta distribution prior distribution Beta(a,b) with a,b>0, the same ordered-sequence marginal likelihood is B(8+a,2+b)/B(a,b). This follows by substituting the normalized prior density into the integral, and shows exactly where the parameter prior distribution changes the Bayes factor. Holding the parameter prior distributions fixed while changing model prior odds leaves that Bayes factor unchanged.

Gaussian practical-null mixture

Words: 79
Bayes factor OurBigBook.com
A Gaussian practical-null mixture compares a narrow centered normal distribution prior with a wider centered normal distribution prior. Neither component is a point mass. With observed mean y∣β∼N(β,1/n) and prior precisions q0​>q1​>0, its model predictive variances are Vi​=1/n+1/qi​, and the Bayes factor is
B01​(y)=V1​/V0​​exp[−y2(V0−1​−V1−1​)/2].
(47)
The overall posterior density is a Bayesian model averaging mixture with component means ny/(n+qi​). A wide-prior penalty can favor the practical null near zero; its dominance depends quantitatively on both prior scales and the observation, not merely on the observation being of order n−1/2.

Savage-Dickey density ratio

Bayes factor OurBigBook.com
For suitable nested models whose common nuisance parameters have matching priors, the Savage-Dickey density ratio expresses a Bayes factor as posterior density divided by prior density at the nested parameter value.

Words: 12

Bayesian model averaging weights each model-specific posterior by that model's posterior probability.
